nameStory: The smoky shrew gets its name from its distinctive grayish-brown fur that has a soft, smoky appearance, especially along its back and sides. Unlike some of its relatives with more contrasting colors, this little mammal looks like it's been lightly dusted with wood smoke or ash.
description: The smoky shrew is a tiny, mouse-sized mammal with a long, pointed snout and beady black eyes. About the size of your thumb, it weighs less than a nickel and has velvety fur that ranges from smoky gray to brownish-gray. Despite its small size, this is actually one of the larger shrews in New England, with a relatively long tail that makes up about half its total length. These energetic little creatures are constantly on the move, searching for insects and other small prey.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Medium-sized for a shrew, roughly thumb-length with a distinctly long, pointed snout that extends well beyond tiny eyes; body feels firm and compact when handled

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Soft, velvety coat in smoky gray to grayish-brown tones; fur feels dense and plush to the touch, with lighter underparts and no sharp color contrasts

idTips.label: Tail
idTips.description: Relatively long tail, about half the total body length, covered in short fur and slightly darker than the body; feels firm and muscular when gently handled

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Tiny four-toed prints in soft mud or snow, each about the size of a pinky nail; tracks often show a bounding pattern with small tail drag marks

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Extremely active and constantly moving in short, quick bursts; makes faint squeaking sounds when disturbed and has a distinctly musky odor

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Small tunnels through leaf litter and tiny scat pellets smaller than rice grains; look for small caches of insect parts under logs or rocks

habitat: Smoky shrews prefer moist, mature forests with thick leaf litter and plenty of fallen logs throughout New England's mountains and hills. They're especially common in mixed hardwood-conifer forests and along the Appalachian Mountains, where cool, humid conditions provide ideal hunting grounds. Look for them in areas with rich, organic soil and dense ground cover that supports abundant insect life.

seasonality.spring: Active throughout the day and night as insects become more abundant; this is when you're most likely to find them foraging in newly thawed leaf litter.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with constant hunting; fur appears sleeker and darker, and they may venture slightly more into open areas during cooler dawn and dusk hours.
seasonality.fall: Busy preparing for winter by caching food and establishing winter territories; fur becomes thicker and more luxurious to the touch.
seasonality.winter: Remain active under snow cover, creating tunnel systems through leaf litter; their high metabolism means they cannot hibernate and must hunt continuously.

funFact: A smoky shrew must eat every 2-3 hours or it will literally starve to death - their heart beats over 1,200 times per minute, making them one of the most metabolically intense mammals on Earth!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the smaller masked shrew, but the smoky shrew is noticeably larger and lacks the sharp color contrast between dark back and light belly that masked shrews display. Memory trick: smoky shrews have 'smoky' (blended) colors while masked shrews look like they're wearing a dark 'mask' over light undergarments.
compareHints: Compared to its relatives, the smoky shrew is larger than both the tiny masked shrew and the even tinier American pygmy shrew, and it lacks the specialized swimming adaptations of the water shrew. Its smoky, uniform coloration is more subdued than the contrasting patterns of masked shrews, and its longer tail helps distinguish it from the shorter-tailed species in the region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Masked shrews are smaller and grayer than the reddish-brown smoky shrew, and much larger than the tiny American pygmy shrew.

Compared to its closest relatives, the American pygmy shrew is noticeably smaller than both the masked shrew and smoky shrew, and lacks the distinctive white belly markings of the eastern water shrew.
Unlike the Masked Shrew which stays on dry land, the Eastern Water Shrew is always found near water and has denser, more water-repellent fur.
